title: Collapsing Dimension
original_question: B = [[1,2],[2,4]] as a function B:R²→R². Line 2y+x=4: apply B → B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2x+4y) = (x+2y, 2(x+2y)). Since x+2y=4 → B maps EVERY point on the line to (4,8)! The whole line collapses to a single point! For any k, 2y+x=k maps to (k,2k). Range of B = {t*(1,2)} — a 1D line! B COLLAPSES a dimension!
core_concept: A singular matrix (det=0) collapses a higher-dimensional space onto a lower-dimensional one. Parallel lines map to different points, but all points on a single line collapse to one output point.

easy.question: What is B*(4,0) for B = [[1,2],[2,4]]?
easy.explanation: Step 1: B*(4,0) = (1*4+2*0, 2*4+4*0) = (4,8). Step 2: Check: 2(0)+4=4, so the point is on the line 2y+x=4, mapping to (4,8). This shows how the matrix transforms individual inputs — and understanding this is the first step to seeing how entire lines collapse.

easy.question: What is B*(2,1) for B = [[1,2],[2,4]]?
easy.explanation: Step 1: B*(2,1) = (1*2+2*1, 2*2+4*1) = (2+2, 4+4) = (4,8). Step 2: Both (4,0) and (2,1) map to the same point (4,8)! This is the hallmark of a singular matrix — different inputs produce identical outputs, meaning information is lost.

easy.question: Both (4,0) and (2,1) map to (4,8) under B = [[1,2],[2,4]]. Why?
options: Both lie on the line 2y+x=4, which collapses to (4,8)
easy.correct_option: Both lie on the line 2y+x=4, which collapses to (4,8)
easy.explanation: Step 1: Check: 2(0)+4=4 and 2(1)+2=4. Step 2: Both points are on the line 2y+x=4, and B collapses this entire line to the single point (4,8). This visual collapse of a line to a point is the geometric meaning of a singular matrix — the null space direction has been squashed to zero.

easy.question: What is the determinant of B = [[1,2],[2,4]]?
easy.explanation: Step 1: det(B) = (1)(4) - (2)(2) = 4 - 4 = 0. Step 2: A zero determinant means B is singular — it collapses dimensions. The determinant measures how much a matrix stretches or squishes space; zero means total collapse in at least one direction.

easy.question: What is the range (output set) of B = [[1,2],[2,4]]?
easy.explanation: Step 1: B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2x+4y) = (x+2y)(1,2). Step 2: The output is always a scalar multiple of (1,2), so the range is the line t(1,2). The column space and range are identical — this 1D line is all that survives the collapse.

easy.question: What dimension does B = [[1,2],[2,4]] map R² onto?
easy.explanation: Step 1: The range is the line t(1,2), which is 1-dimensional. Step 2: B collapses the 2D input onto a 1D output — it loses one dimension. This is exactly what rank-nullity predicts: rank 1 + nullity 1 = 2.

easy.question: Does the line 2y+x=10 map to a single point under B?
options: different points map to different outputs
easy.explanation: Step 1: For any (x,y) on 2y+x=10, B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2x+4y) = (10, 20). Step 2: The entire line maps to the single point (10,20). This pattern — lines collapsing to points — is the signature of a rank-1 matrix in 2D.

easy.question: What does a zero determinant tell us about the matrix?
options: The matrix is singular and collapses dimensions
The matrix maps everything to zero
easy.correct_option: The matrix is singular and collapses dimensions
easy.explanation: Step 1: det=0 means the matrix is singular (not invertible). Step 2: A singular matrix maps the input space onto a lower-dimensional subspace, collapsing some dimensions. This is why zero determinant is equivalent to information loss.

easy.question: B*(0,0) = ?
easy.explanation: Step 1: B*(0,0) = (1*0+2*0, 2*0+4*0) = (0,0). Step 2: Any linear transformation maps the origin to the origin. This is a fundamental property — linearity requires T(0) = 0.

easy.question: The line 2y+x=k maps to the point (k, 2k). What does k=0 give?
easy.explanation: Step 1: When k=0, the line 2y+x=0 passes through the origin. Step 2: B maps every point on this line to (0,0) — the entire line collapses to the origin. This line is precisely the null space of B, the direction along which all information is lost.

medium.question: Why does B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2(x+2y)) always have the form (a, 2a)?
options: Because the second component is always exactly twice the first
medium.correct_option: Because the second component is always exactly twice the first
medium.explanation: Step 1: B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2x+4y) = (x+2y, 2(x+2y)). Step 2: The second component is always 2 times the first, so all outputs lie on the line y=2x (or direction (1,2)). This is why the range is a line, not a plane — the matrix forces every output into this single direction.

medium.question: If 2y+x=4 maps to (4,8) and 2y+x=10 maps to (10,20), what general rule emerges?
options: All lines map to the same point
medium.explanation: Step 1: For any (x,y) on 2y+x=k, B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2(x+2y)) = (k, 2k). Step 2: Each distinct k gives a distinct output point (k, 2k) on the range line. This rule — lines map to points — is the geometric essence of dimensional collapse.

medium.question: Are different values of k mapped to different output points (k, 2k)?
options: Yes — different k values give different points on the line t(1,2)
— all map to the same point
Only for positive k — does t match
Only for integers — does t match
medium.correct_option: Yes — different k values give different points on the line t(1,2)
medium.explanation: Step 1: If k₁ ≠ k₂, then (k₁, 2k₁) ≠ (k₂, 2k₂). Step 2: Each parallel line 2y+x=k maps to a distinct point on the range, preserving information about which line the input was on. B loses information along the line (position within each parallel class) but retains information between lines.

medium.question: What information does B lose when it collapses the line 2y+x=4 to (4,8)?
options: Where exactly on the line the input was located
The value of k (which line the input is on)
The output value — does t match
thing is lost — does t match
medium.correct_option: Where exactly on the line the input was located
medium.explanation: Step 1: All points on 2y+x=4 give the same output (4,8). Step 2: B loses the information about which specific point on the line was the input — the position along the direction perpendicular to (1,2) is lost. This is precisely the null space direction (2,-1).

medium.question: What is the dimension of the null space of B = [[1,2],[2,4]]?
medium.explanation: Step 1: B is 2×2 with rank 1 (since the second row is twice the first). Step 2: By rank-nullity: nullity = 2-1 = 1. The null space is a 1D line — the direction along which information vanishes completely.

medium.question: What direction is the null space of B = [[1,2],[2,4]]?
medium.explanation: Step 1: Solve B*(x,y) = (0,0): x+2y=0 -> x=-2y. Step 2: Setting y=-1 gives x=2, so the null space direction is (2,-1). Moving along this direction produces zero output — it is the 'blind spot' of the matrix.

medium.question: Is the null space direction (2,-1) perpendicular to the range direction (1,2)?
medium.explanation: Step 1: (2,-1)·(1,2) = 2(1)+(-1)(2) = 2-2 = 0. Step 2: The null space and range are always perpendicular — this is a fundamental property. The direction that gets collapsed is always orthogonal to the direction that survives.

medium.question: If B collapses 2D to 1D, how many dimensions are lost?
options: All of them — does t match
medium.explanation: Step 1: The input is 2D and the output is 1D. Step 2: 2-1 = 1 dimension is lost — exactly the dimension of the null space. This is the rank-nullity theorem in action: what you lose (nullity) plus what you keep (rank) equals what you started with.

medium.question: Why can't we recover the original input from B*(x,y)?
options: Because many different inputs give the same output (not one-to-one)
Because the output is always positive
medium.correct_option: Because many different inputs give the same output (not one-to-one)
medium.explanation: Step 1: All points on a line 2y+x=k map to the same output (k,2k). Step 2: From the output alone, you can determine k but not which specific point on the line was the input. This non-invertibility is why singular matrices cannot be undone.

medium.question: The range of B is the line t(1,2). Is this line the same as the column space of B?
options: Yes — the range and column space are the same thing
Only if B is square — does t match
medium.correct_option: Yes — the range and column space are the same thing
medium.explanation: Step 1: The column space is span{(1,2),(2,4)} = span{(1,2)} since (2,4)=2(1,2). Step 2: The range is {B*(x,y)} = {t(1,2)}. They are identical. The column space is just another name for the range — the set of all possible outputs.

hard.question: Prove that all points on the line 2y+x=k map to the same point under B = [[1,2],[2,4]].
options: For any (x,y) with x+2y=k: B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2(x+2y)) = (k, 2k), which is the same for all such (x,y)
This is only true for k=4
Only integer points map to the same point
hard.correct_option: For any (x,y) with x+2y=k: B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2(x+2y)) = (k, 2k), which is the same for all such (x,y)
hard.explanation: Step 1: B*(x,y) = (x+2y, 2x+4y) = (x+2y, 2(x+2y)). Step 2: If x+2y=k, then B*(x,y) = (k, 2k) regardless of which specific (x,y) on the line is used. This proof shows why singular matrices collapse lines: the matrix only 'sees' the component along (1,2), not the component along (2,-1).

hard.question: Why does B lose information specifically along the direction (2,-1)?
options: Because (2,-1) is the null space direction — B*(2,-1) = (0,0), so any displacement along this direction is invisible in the output
Because B can't handle negative numbers
Because the diagonal entries are positive
hard.correct_option: Because (2,-1) is the null space direction — B*(2,-1) = (0,0), so any displacement along this direction is invisible in the output
hard.explanation: Step 1: B*(2,-1) = (2-2, 4-4) = (0,0). Step 2: Moving along (2,-1) produces zero output, so B cannot distinguish between points that differ only in this direction. The null space direction is the dimension that is completely invisible to the matrix.

hard.question: How many distinct parallel lines 2y+x=k are there, and how many distinct output points do they map to?
options: Infinitely many lines, each mapping to a distinct point (k,2k) on the range line
Infinitely many lines, all mapping to one point
Finitely many lines — does t match
One line mapping to one point
hard.correct_option: Infinitely many lines, each mapping to a distinct point (k,2k) on the range line
hard.explanation: Step 1: k can be any real number, giving infinitely many parallel lines. Step 2: Each k maps to a unique point (k,2k), so there are infinitely many distinct output points, one per line. This one-to-one correspondence between parallel lines and output points is how the matrix preserves some information while losing other information.

hard.question: For B = [[1,2],[2,4]], what is the preimage of (6,12)?
hard.explanation: Step 1: (6,12) = (k,2k) with k=6. Step 2: The preimage is the line 2y+x=6 — all points that B maps to (6,12). For singular matrices, preimages are always lines (or higher-dimensional sets), never single points.

hard.question: Can a non-singular (invertible) matrix ever collapse a line to a single point?
options: No — non-singular matrices are one-to-one and preserve dimensions
hard.correct_option: No — non-singular matrices are one-to-one and preserve dimensions
hard.explanation: Step 1: A non-singular matrix has det!=0 and full rank. Step 2: It maps distinct inputs to distinct outputs (one-to-one), so no information is lost and dimensions are preserved. This is the key distinction: non-singular matrices are invertible, singular matrices are not.

hard.question: If the range of B is 1D and the input is 2D, what is the rank-nullity relationship?
hard.explanation: Step 1: Rank = dim(range) = 1. Step 2: Nullity = dim(null space) = 1. By rank-nullity: 1+1=2 = n. The input dimension is split between what the matrix keeps (rank) and what it destroys (nullity).

hard.question: What would B = [[1,2],[2,4]] look like if we changed it to [[1,2],[2,5]]?
options: It would no longer be singular — det=1≠0, so it would be invertible and preserve dimensions
It would map everything to zero
It would have rank 0 — does t match
hard.correct_option: It would no longer be singular — det=1≠0, so it would be invertible and preserve dimensions
hard.explanation: Step 1: det([[1,2],[2,5]]) = 5-4 = 1 != 0. Step 2: With non-zero determinant, the matrix is invertible, one-to-one, and maps R² onto R² — no collapsing. This shows how a tiny change (4 to 5) can completely eliminate dimensional collapse.

hard.question: Geometrically, what does B = [[1,2],[2,4]] do to the unit square in R²?
options: It squishes the square flat onto the line t(1,2), collapsing one dimension
hard.correct_option: It squishes the square flat onto the line t(1,2), collapsing one dimension
hard.explanation: Step 1: The unit square has corners at (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1). Step 2: B maps these to (0,0), (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) — all on the line t(1,2). The square collapses to a line segment, showing how area (2D) becomes length (1D).

hard.question: If B maps 2D to 1D, what does B² map to?
options: Still 1D — once collapsed, further applications can't collapse more
hard.correct_option: Still 1D — once collapsed, further applications can't collapse more
hard.explanation: Step 1: B already maps everything onto the 1D line t(1,2). Step 2: Applying B again just maps points on this line to points on the same line — it can't collapse further since it's already 1D. Once a dimension is lost, it stays lost: B² has the same rank as B.

hard.question: Why is the ability of a singular matrix to 'collapse' dimensions significant in applications?
options: It represents irreversible information loss — compression, projection, and dimensionality reduction all rely on this
hard.correct_option: It represents irreversible information loss — compression, projection, and dimensionality reduction all rely on this
hard.explanation: Step 1: Singular matrices map higher-dimensional data to lower dimensions. Step 2: This irreversible loss is exactly what happens in image compression, 3D-to-2D projection, and PCA — useful features are kept, redundant information is collapsed. Understanding which dimensions collapse and which survive is the key to mastering linear algebra.

real_life_application.title: 3D to 2D Photo
real_life_application.story: When you take a photo, the 3D world is projected onto a flat 2D sensor. Millions of points at different depths all land on the same spot in the image — the depth dimension is collapsed, just like a singular matrix collapses a dimension.
real_life_application.question: When a camera collapses 3D onto 2D, which mathematical concept does this represent?
options: A singular matrix mapping higher dimensions to lower dimensions
real_life_application.correct_option: A singular matrix mapping higher dimensions to lower dimensions
real_life_application.explanation: Step 1: The camera's projection matrix is singular — it maps 3D points to 2D. Step 2: Points at different depths (along the null space direction) all produce the same 2D image point, losing depth information. This is why photos cannot reconstruct the full 3D scene — the depth dimension has been irreversibly collapsed.

real_life_application.title: Data Compression
real_life_application.concept: PCA reduces dimensions by discarding null space
real_life_application.story: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduces data dimensionality by keeping only the directions of highest variance. The discarded directions form the null space of the compression — like a singular matrix, it collapses many dimensions into fewer.
real_life_application.question: In PCA dimensionality reduction, what mathematical concept represents the directions that are dropped?
options: The null space of the compression
real_life_application.correct_option: The null space of the compression
real_life_application.explanation: Step 1: PCA keeps high-variance directions (the range) and discards low-variance directions (the null space). Step 2: Like a singular matrix, it collapses data onto a lower-dimensional subspace, losing information along the null space. This is why PCA is both powerful and dangerous — discarding too much can lose critical features.

real_life_application.title: Shadow Projection
real_life_application.story: When sunlight casts a shadow of a 3D object onto a flat wall, the shadow is a 2D projection — one dimension (depth relative to the wall) is lost. Every point along the line from the object to the wall produces the same shadow point.
real_life_application.question: When a 3D object casts a 2D shadow, what happens to the depth dimension?
options: It is collapsed — points at different depths produce the same shadow point
real_life_application.correct_option: It is collapsed — points at different depths produce the same shadow point
real_life_application.explanation: Step 1: The shadow projection maps 3D points to 2D. Step 2: Points along the light direction (the null space of the projection) all produce the same shadow point — the depth is lost. This is why shadows cannot show the full shape of an object.

real_life_application.title: Map Projection
real_life_application.concept: Earth's surface projected onto flat map
real_life_application.story: Cartographers project the Earth's 3D surface onto a flat 2D map. This projection is a singular transformation — it collapses the altitude dimension, distorting areas near the poles. The Mercator projection stretches some areas while compressing others.
real_life_application.question: When projecting the Earth's 3D surface onto a flat map, what information is inevitably lost?
real_life_application.explanation: Step 1: The map projection maps 3D surface points to 2D coordinates. Step 2: Altitude is collapsed — mountains and valleys appear as flat points on the map, just as a singular matrix collapses one dimension. This is why no flat map can perfectly represent the Earth.

real_life_application.title: Survey Aggregation
real_life_application.concept: Many responses collapsed to summary statistics
real_life_application.story: When a company surveys thousands of customers and summarizes the results as a few average scores, many individual responses are collapsed into single summary values. This aggregation is like a singular matrix — individual variation is lost.
real_life_application.question: When thousands of survey responses are summarized as a few average scores, what happens to individual variation?
options: It is collapsed — individual differences are lost in the aggregation
real_life_application.correct_option: It is collapsed — individual differences are lost in the aggregation
real_life_application.explanation: Step 1: The summary operation maps many data points to a few statistics. Step 2: Individual responses that differ but have the same average produce the same output — like points on a line collapsing to one point. This is why averages alone cannot reveal the full story.

real_life_application.title: Audio Downsampling
real_life_application.story: When audio is downsampled from 44.1 kHz to 22 kHz, high-frequency information above the Nyquist limit is collapsed and lost. This is a dimensionality reduction — the audio signal is projected onto a lower-dimensional subspace.
real_life_application.question: When audio is downsampled, what happens to high-frequency information above the Nyquist limit?
options: It is collapsed and lost — like a singular matrix discarding dimensions
It is shifted to low frequencies
real_life_application.correct_option: It is collapsed and lost — like a singular matrix discarding dimensions
real_life_application.explanation: Step 1: Downsampling reduces the sampling rate, lowering the dimensionality of the audio signal. Step 2: High-frequency components in the null space of the downsampling operation are lost — they cannot be recovered. This is why professional audio uses higher sample rates.
